text: Cassini was sent to end its life by diving into Saturn because if it were left alone it would eventually hit a moon. Saturn’s moons, especially Enceladus, could have places where life might exist, and a stray probe from Earth could carry microbes or other Earth stuff that would contaminate the surface. By the end of the mission, Cassini had little fuel left and could not stay in stable orbit forever. Crashing into Saturn was the safe way to finish, letting scientists get final data near the planet. The main reason is to protect the moons from possible Earth contamination.

Your stationary leg hurts because that is the one doing nearly all the work when you ride. You might think both legs share the effort, but when one foot is on the board and the other is kicking or planted, the planted leg is holding your whole body up and absorbing the bumps. That is why it aches. The kicking leg gets a workout too, but the stationary leg carries more of the weight and vibration. If you ride with your dominant foot forward, your other leg is the one pushing, but your dominant or stationary leg is still bracing the board against the ground.

I know this sounds simple but people often expect both legs to feel the same. They do not. Think of it like balancing on a curb. The leg that stays on the board is doing the balancing and shock absorption, and that is the one that gets tired. If your left leg is your stationary one, that left leg takes most of the strain. The silk thing, if you mean the board deck or your socks, does not change the fact that the planted foot is working much harder than the one pushing.

It also hurts because the joints get loaded. When you ride, the knee and hip of the stationary leg stay bent for a long time, and the shock from the wheels goes straight through that side. The kicking leg gets a pump, but the stationary leg is taking the repeated jolts. That is why after a long ride your stationary leg can feel stiff or sore.

One more thing. People often blame their stance, but really it is just that one leg is doing most of the job. You do not need fancy gear to fix it. You can switch which foot goes forward sometimes so the load changes sides. If your stationary leg is always the same one, it gets overworked. So try alternating. If you ride for a long time and your stationary leg hurts, that is your body telling you the same side has been taking all the impact.

It also depends on how fast and how long you ride. A short ride might feel fine, but after twenty or thirty minutes the stationary leg will ache. That is not damage, just normal fatigue. Let it rest, walk it off, and maybe switch your front foot. Your body will stop treating the stationary leg like a shock absorber.

It just works that way, and most people only figure it out after they have been hurting for a while.

its about ancestry not where they live now. most african americans are from west and central africa originally, brought over as enslaved people and their families stayed in the usa for generations, so the label afro american or african american is meant to tie them to that origin rather than say they are still living there. its a way of naming that shared heritage. lots of people born and raised in the us answer to it because that heritage connects them to africa. if someone was born in africa recently it would be different, but the term doesnt mean they moved over from there yesterday. i know it sounds odd if you read it literally, but the label is about roots not current address. its less about where you were born and more about the common origin the label points to. people have debated the word too, some prefer black american or other terms, but the african american part is meant to acknowledge that connection to africa even when the family has been in the us for many generations. its a historical label, not a statement about recent migration.

the thing is, drugs that hit the pleasure centre don't just turn a dial up, they change how the body regulates its own chemical system. natural dopamine pathways have feedback loops that keep things balanced. when you overload that system repeatedly, the balance shifts. the body tries to compensate, which is the root of tolerance. so the same drug that feels good now can demand bigger doses over time. and then you have withdrawal, where the system is left out of whack and the person feels awful without it. that is why the bad effects come from the mechanism, not from a bad ingredient being mixed in. i don't think there is a natural or made drug that gives intense pleasure with zero adverse effects, because any drug strong enough to make you feel great will disturb the equilibrium the brain relies on. you can have something mild that is less risky, but the moment it produces intense euphoria it is pushing past what the body expects, and the body pushes back. that is what creates the dependence and the crash. people who say the drug itself is always the problem miss that point. it's the interaction with the reward system. so no, the bad stuff is not an extra flaw, it is built into how pleasure chemistry works.

you did not send the actual list so i am guessing from the subject line. the basics are what really matter here. get a mortgage in principle before looking at anything else because it tells you what you can afford and stops you wasting time. when you find the place, have a proper survey done, not just the quick lender one. A survey catches defects that could be expensive to fix later. dont forget the deposit, insurance and a small fund for repairs after moving in. Also budget for extra costs: conveyance, legal fees, survey fee, and a little cash for moving day. Negotiate on price if the survey finds problems. If you have no problems, still get the legal work started early because completion can take weeks. you can also ask the estate agent what they know about the street, but confirm the important bits with your solicitor. One thing people miss is the difference between fixtures and fittings, the stuff attached to the house usually stays, but moveable items do not, so write anything you want included into the contract. Its easier to check everything now than argue later.

Hi,
the main difference is that the 3-in-1 is a compromise on chemistry. Individual products use specific surfactants and pH levels built for one job. A dedicated shampoo is made to clean hair without leaving it tangled, and a bodywash has a different chemical makeup for skin. The surfactants in a 3-in-1 are a mix of anionic and non-ionic types to handle both hair and skin, unlike the specific ones in the individual bottles. Basically the 3-in-1 is a middle ground that tries to be all things to all users, but the tradeoff is a weaker formula.

When you mix them into one bottle it has to be milder to work on both. This means its not really doing a proper job at any single one. The 3-in-1 blends the needs of hair and body, so you lose the specific active ingredients that make the individual counterparts work.

that is also the difference from the 2-in-1. A 2-in-1 is strictly for hair, so its surfactants are targeted for the scalp and strands. The 3-in-1 has to cater to the whole body, meaning the formula is a broader blend that cant be as harsh or as specific. I wouldnt bother using the 3-in-1 for either task. You end up with less clean hair and skin that feels dry or tight. The dedicated products are better if you want actual results. The 3-in-1 just saves space on a shelf.

I know this looks impossible because nothing around us is moving, but its real and measurable. The main tool now is GPS. They put stations on the plates and look at how their position changes over years. You can do this with ordinary receivers and the accuracy is millimetre level if you process it properly. A single reading tells you nothing. You need at least a few years of data before the trend becomes clear.

Satellite laser ranging does the same thing, by measuring how far away a satellite is from the ground station. InSAR lets you see ground deformation between radar passes, which is useful for smaller scale or volcanic areas. For long baselines, VLBI can track the rotation of Earth itself.

Your friend can check the results on the web. The big picture is that plates move centimetres per year, and you can see the trend even in short time spans. you dont need to be a geologist to look at a chart and see the line drifting.

I wouldnt bother calculating it yourself unless you really want to. The data is public and you can see the same trend in a few clicks.

When people in a family group are related, their kids can get the same hidden problems from both parents. Humans carry recessive genes that dont show up in healthy adults. when relatives have a child, the chance both copies match goes way up.

Many small genes affect IQ, not one single gene. Inbreeding makes harmful recessive versions show up more often. Its not that the parents are stupid. The science part is that identical bad copies are more likely to meet, and that adds up across the many genes involved in brain development. This risk goes up with how close the relation is.

Its a risk, not a guarantee. Two first cousins having a kid is worse than two unrelated people. Most inbred lines dont all come out the same. The lower average IQ shows up because the population gets more of those bad recessive genes, not because one bad gene is responsible.

Pain isn't spread evenly across the body, so the arm just isn't one of the most sensitive places. Fingertips, lips, and the area around the ribs have a much higher concentration of pain nerve endings, so even a small cut or tap registers more sharply there. The arm, particularly the upper arm, is padded with a thicker layer of fat and muscle. That extra tissue acts like a cushion and spreads the force of a hit or stab over a larger area instead of concentrating it in one spot. Bone is also farther from the skin than in the fingers, so impacts don't translate directly to nerve endings the same way. The net result is that the arm often feels milder for the same kind of injury. That's why a bruise on your bicep can be less dramatic than the same thing happening to a finger or your side. In short, the arm isn't less damaged, the body just reads it as less intense.

Carbon monoxide is dangerous mainly because it stops the blood from carrying oxygen. When you breathe it in, it grabs onto hemoglobin in the red blood cells and holds on very tightly. That blocks oxygen from doing its job. Carbon dioxide, by contrast, is a normal product of metabolism. At everyday levels, the body is built to handle it, and the lungs simply exchange it with oxygen.

The key difference is how each gas interacts with hemoglobin. CO has a much stronger attraction to hemoglobin than O2 does. In simple terms, once it is in the blood, it does not leave easily. This is what causes the silent problem with CO. The person feels ill, dizzy, and weak because the tissues are starved of oxygen, but the blood may still look normal. CO2 is not usually a threat at ordinary room concentrations. It can become a problem at high concentrations, but that is a different kind of danger, more about the air being too thick and irritating or asphyxiating, not about blocking oxygen transport in the blood.

Another part of the answer is exposure level. CO can be lethal at low, barely noticeable concentrations, which is why detectors exist. CO2 at normal outdoor levels is not something you have to worry about. You only need to think about it in very enclosed spaces, like a basement or a small room with many people, where it can build up. So it is not that CO2 is completely harmless, but it is far less immediately threatening to a healthy person in normal conditions.

For a new colleague, the useful takeaway is this: CO is poisonous because it quietly blocks oxygen delivery. CO2 is part of normal breathing and is only dangerous when it accumulates to high levels. That is the core of the difference, and it is also why CO needs constant detection in places where it can build up, such as garages, kitchens, or anywhere combustion happens.

When a plane hits something hard, the seat belts stop your lower body but your head and shoulders keep moving forward. That motion is what causes most of the bad injuries, like the head striking the seat in front of you or a hard neck snap. The brace position is meant to stop that. You put your hands behind your back or on your stomach, tuck your head down, and press your body against the seat. That way you hold yourself tight and limit the forward swing of the head.

Its not that the brace position prevents the crash from happening. What it does is reduce the chance of a serious neck or head injury during the impact. For a new hire, the main point is simple: in an emergency, you sit as far back as possible, hold on with both hands, tuck the head, and stay in that posture until its over. The idea is just to keep the body compact against the seat so nothing whips around inside the cabin.

Most pre-industrial enterprises were local and small, so they rarely left the kind of records or brand identity that later allowed companies to become famous. Before factories, railroads, and mass media, business knowledge stayed within guilds, families, or towns. When records were kept, they were often handwritten ledgers or legal charters, not advertisements or public marketing.

The Medici banking family is an example of a well-known pre-industrial business, but such cases were exceptional. Industrialisation changed things by creating larger companies, centralised management, and wider distribution, which made firms easier to recognise across regions and later across countries. That is why familiar names usually trace back to the industrial era or shortly after it.

I keep seeing ads where the dealership says its rate is lower than the bank, and that is exactly why I ended up with the bank. The interest rate is only one number in a messy total. The dealer can show me a low number on paper while quietly adding charges, add-on products, and a longer loan term.

The first concrete thing I noticed was that the dealer's low rate was only good for a short promotional window. After that, the rate climbed up. I did not want to be stuck paying a higher rate for most of the loan. The bank quote I got was steadier, and the total I would pay over the life of the loan was smaller.

Then there were the dealer extras. They offered an extended warranty, a paint sealant, a security package, and a fee for processing. Each one looked optional, but the salesperson kept putting them on the final sheet. Even when I removed most of them, the doc fee and registration charges still pushed the total up. The bank did not try to sell me extras with the loan. I only had to pay the bank's own fees, which were smaller and easier to see.

My position is that the advertised rate is easy to hide costs behind. A lower rate means little if the term is longer or the payment starts from a high amount due. I looked at total interest, not just the rate. The bank was not necessarily the lowest rate, but it was the lowest total cost.

What I would tell anyone in this situation is to ask for the itemized total from both places and compare the total interest and fees. Do not let the monthly payment be the only number you care about. The monthly payment can be made to look cheap by stretching the term, and that is often more expensive overall. The bank loan I took had a clearer fee structure and a smaller amount due from start to finish.

It is frustrating that the dealership can make the rate sound better while the final bill is higher. I would not pay extra for extras and a longer term just because the sticker said low rate. For me, the bank was cheaper because it gave me a simple loan without the dealer's extra costs. That is why I chose it.

My take is that the difference that really matters is between medical and recreational rules. States that allow medical marijuana usually need a doctor's note and limit how you can use it. Recreational legality is separate and newer, and not every state has caught up. I think this makes sense because medicine and fun use have different risks. The state controls are there to manage who gets access, not just whether anyone can buy it. If you live in a medical-only state, you may be able to get it for specific conditions without being able to buy it casually. That gap is the detail people overlook.

Our bodies don't store electricity like batteries. The useful signals come from ions moving across cell membranes. Nerve and heart muscle cells maintain different concentrations of sodium and potassium. When a nerve fires, sodium channels open and positive charge flows in, creating an action potential. That gradient is maintained by pumps that burn energy. It is not a spark we can feel; it is a chemical gradient doing electrical work. So the body does not create electricity from nothing. It converts stored chemical energy into brief electrical messages, which is why a beating heart or a twitching finger is really ion traffic.

I still get asked how people actually pull samples out of old records, so here is how I think about it.

When someone samples an older song, they are not playing the song again. They are lifting a small piece of the original recording. A break beat, a vocal phrase, a bass line, a drum fill. You take that piece, cut it to length, maybe slow it down, change its pitch, and build a new track around it. The sampled sound stays the recorded performance, not a fresh take by the new artist. That distinction is the whole point.

The practical side is simpler than people think. You need the source audio in a usable digital format. That means ripping a CD or recording vinyl into a computer, then working in a sequencer or sampler. From there, you can loop a two or four bar section, adjust tempo, flip it, reverse it, or chop it into smaller hits. Many tracks start with just one isolated element and grow from there. I have watched producers find the exact drum break they want, trim it, and then spend an hour getting the loop to sit right.

Sampling also has a legal side that matters more than the music side. If you use a recognizable part of someone elses recording, you generally need permission. That means contacting the copyright owner or licensing agency, and paying for the right to use it. Some people try to hide it by reversing the clip or burying it in a mix, but that does not make it less copyrighted.

I think the mistake people make is treating sampling like a shortcut. It is not. A good sample choice changes a track completely. The old recording carries its own feel, and that is what the new artist is after. The work is in knowing which fragment to take and how much to change it. Sometimes just slowing a 1970s funk break down to half speed is enough to make a brand new beat.

My head hurts with a headache because the pain doesn't start in the skull. The bones have very few pain fibers, so they can't be the source. What does hurt are the membranes that cover the brain and the blood vessels and small nerves around them. When those get stretched or irritated, the trigeminal nerve carries the signal to the brain, and the brain reads it as pain. If the vessels swell and press on the membranes, the pain signal gets stronger. That's why a headache can build slowly instead of hitting all at once.

For me, it usually comes after a day of bad sleep, no water, and too much screen time. I can feel my neck and jaw go tight, and that pressure seems to make the headache worse. So if you're asking why your head hurts: it's your nervous system flagging irritation in the soft tissues, not the hard shell.

I can’t tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday and chose this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and figured it would be easy. We entered our names into their completely useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15. It was a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn’t wasted. It was an absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

The space bar rattles. I hit it with the edge of my thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists dont ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well the under-21 version, so I've sat through a lot of shows before I could gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

Good part: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You're basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view, rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too. The strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers, those people are athletes. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a rip-off way exactly, just that if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don't know. There's a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. Also, there's way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't really pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear over the phone. The sales representative wrote down the delivery address incorrectly, and her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. Our address should have been 5407, but the package went to 5401. The people at 5401 took it to the local UPS store to send it back. The package was never seen again. We did not know what had happened for several weeks. During the dispute, we placed another order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. The owner was handling the matter at that point. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but said we would not get a refund unless the shirts were returned. He also said we had not been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, which was four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company, and we got a credit in the end.
